The Garante learned through a report that the municipality of Orte had installed video surveillance cameras without ensuring transparency towards data subjects. The investigation found 43 cameras, operated without a sufficient legal basis, with deficient information notices and no data protection impact assessment, and the municipality also failed to fully and promptly answer the Authority's information requests. The Garante declared the processing unlawful and imposed a fine of EUR 5,000 for the video surveillance conduct and EUR 1,000 for the failure to cooperate, EUR 6,000 in total. No further corrective measures were ordered because the cameras were no longer active, and the order is to be published.

The DPA issued a warning to the controller for violating Articles 5(1)(c), 15(1) and (3) and 12(2) and (6) GDPR by failing to provide access to the data subject’s personal data and by requiring unnecessary additional information for access.

The DPA ordered the operator of a live-streaming website to change their cookie banner due to its deceptive design. The DPA considered the “accept” option to be visually more prominent, unlawfully nudging users towards consent.

Romania's data protection authority, acting as lead authority, investigated Klass Wagen S.R.L. after the company notified a personal data breach and the authority received a referral. A former employee had disclosed colleagues' credentials for the contract management system, which allowed unauthorised access to the personal data of a very large number of customers and employees, including people in other EU/EEA states. The incident was reported late internally, so no immediate measures were taken. The authority found a breach of Art. 32(1)(b) and (d) and (2) GDPR, fined the company 35,615 lei (about EUR 7,000), and ordered it to put in place a procedure for revoking access rights and deactivating former employees' accounts.

The DPA imposed a €1,000 fine on a controller for unlawfully refusing to provide access to a data subject. The DPA found that the request was not abusive, unfounded or would adversely affect the rights and freedoms of others.

The DPA held that, even though a complaint against a medical doctor, who had allegedly accessed medical files without authorization, was later withdrawn, his failure to cooperate with the DPA still justified issuing a reprimand.

The Spanish AEPD sanctioned the airport operator AENA for running a voluntary facial-recognition system for passengers to access airport areas without a valid data protection impact assessment. The assessment did not justify necessity and proportionality, was not updated, and processing went ahead despite two unfavourable reports from the AEPD. The Agency found an infringement of Article 35 GDPR and imposed a fine of EUR 10,043,002. It also confirmed the temporary suspension of all biometric processing until AENA carries out a proper impact assessment.
The DPA found a violation of a former pupil’s right to erasure because a regional education authority failed to delete their records after they completed compulsory schooling.

The DPA imposed a €150 fine on an inspector of the State Police for unlawfully obtaining a citizen’s personal data from the database of the Ministry of the Interior, and sharing it in a Discord group.

At the end of 2024 a large personal data leak affecting almost all Latvian municipalities was found; the data were stored in an information system run by ZZ Dats. The Data State Inspectorate inspected and found that the company breached Article 32 GDPR because it had not sufficiently ensured that processor obligations were met. It imposed an administrative fine of EUR 300,000, calculated under the Inspectorate's methodology based on EDPB guidelines. The company has appealed to the Riga City Court. The municipalities involved received reprimands for insufficient oversight of the processor.

The DPA held that a publisher of console games could comply with an access request by providing a user with remote access via their user account. However, the DPA found that information was incomplete and found a violation of Article 15 GDPR.

The DPA fined a controller €1,500 for unlawfully recording a public sidewalk with a CCTV camera and for publishing images of a suspected thief on social media, thereby breaching the principles of data minimisation and transparency, as well as the rules governing the processing of criminal data.

The DPA held that a public service broadcaster lawfully required users to login to a streaming service in order to offer a personalised experience. According to the DPA, the processing of users’ data was necessary for the public interest and was covered by users’ expectations.

The Polish data protection authority opened proceedings of its own motion against a court bailiff after being told that personal data had been disclosed to an unauthorised recipient. The bailiff had neither reported the breach to the authority within 72 hours nor notified the person whose data was disclosed. The President of UODO found infringements of Articles 33(1) and 34(1)-(2) GDPR and imposed two separate fines, PLN 7,700 and PLN 13,200 (PLN 20,900 in total). The bailiff was also ordered to notify the affected person within 3 days with the information required by Article 34(2).

Parents complained that a secondary school published on its website a circular convening an extraordinary class council for disciplinary proceedings against their son, with the pupil's surname in the file name. The Garante found unlawful dissemination of a minor's data without a legal basis (Art. 5(1)(a), 6 GDPR, Art. 2-ter Code) and a failure to appoint a DPO and notify contact details until after the proceedings began (Art. 37(1) and (7)). The complaint-related Art. 12 charge was dropped as the school removed the file promptly in good faith. Two separate fines of EUR 2,000 each were imposed, totalling EUR 4,000, with publication of the order.

A former employee of the municipality of Curtarolo complained that CCTV footage and a video filmed by a private individual on the mayor's instruction were used against her in disciplinary proceedings, and that the municipality's CCTV system lacked proper signage and compliance. The Garante found unlawful processing on two separate conducts: street CCTV without a valid legal basis, proper information notices or a DPIA, and use of video in the employment context for disciplinary purposes without labour-law safeguards, including investigative filming outside working hours. It imposed fines of EUR 5,000 and EUR 10,000, totalling EUR 15,000, and ordered publication. No further corrective measures were ordered since the conduct had ceased and the municipality said it had taken remedial steps.

A man complained that an online news article about his criminal conviction was still available long after the events, and that the publisher ignored his request of August 2024 to exercise his rights. The publisher's website had no privacy policy or contact details, and the publisher also ignored the Garante's request for information. The article was de-indexed and a privacy policy was published only after proceedings began. The Garante found violations of Article 12(1), (2) and (3) GDPR and Article 157 of the Italian Code, ordered the publisher to put in place measures to facilitate data subject requests, and fined it EUR 20,000.

A person complained that the Latina Bar Association's website published a court hearing schedule PDF containing personal data of the complainant and others, including data on criminal offences and proceedings. The PDF, listing 18 defendants and 4 defence lawyers, stayed online and was indexed by search engines for a long period. The Bar Association blamed human error during the Covid-19 emergency. The Garante found the processing unlawful, lacking a legal basis and breaching the lawfulness principle and Article 10, and imposed a fine of EUR 15,000. No further corrective measures were ordered because the online dissemination had ended.

The DPA fined the Italian public broadcast €150,000 for airing a private conversation of a former Minister involved in a political scandal. The DPA held that broadcasting the conversation was not essential to the journalistic activities of the controller.

The DPA found that the Moderate Party's national organization unlawfully processed personal data with the distribution of personal video greetings, via SMS or email, ahead of an upcoming election. Amongst other things, the political party failed to inform data subjects about the processing of their data.

The DPA found that the Sweden Democrats unlawfully sent text messages advertising for votes in an upcoming election. Amongst other things, the political party failed to inform data subjects about the processing of their data.

ANSPDCP concluded an investigation in September 2025 into the electricity producer and supplier Hidroelectrica, started after the company notified a personal data breach. A technical error in the IT system used to send invoices caused a customer to receive an invoice belonging to another person, so several customers' data were disclosed without authorisation. The authority found a breach of Article 32(1)(b) and (d) and (4) GDPR and fined the company RON 25,392 (about EUR 5,000).

Experian Nederland, a credit information bureau, offered a Credit Check service until 1 January 2025 that supplied creditworthiness scores on consumers to its clients. In a primary decision of 6 December 2023 the AP fined it for lacking a valid legal basis (legitimate interest) and for not informing data subjects adequately, and also imposed two penalty orders. On objection, the AP upheld the objection formally, revoked the primary decision and imposed a new fine of EUR 2,700,000 for the same infringements. Experian acknowledged the infringement, stopped its Dutch activities and will delete its database; the press release says it will not appeal.

The DPA imposed a combined £14,000,000 fine on a business services provider and its processor, following a cyber attack which gave unauthorised parties access to over 6 million people’s data. The DPA found a lack of appropriate security measures.

The DPA held that a credit information agency failed to provide a data subject access to the logic involved in its automated credit scoring and to sources and recipients of the data subject’s personal data.

The DPA ordered a media company to remove a data subject’s image from online articles and to replace their name with initials since the publication caused excessive harm to the person while the public interest in the depicted events diminished over time.
The DPA issued a warning to a controller along with an order to provide two patients with information on their medical treatment after failing to respond to their access requests.

ANSPDCP concluded an investigation in September 2025 into an online shop operator, Vellea Home SRL, which had notified a personal data breach after a cyber attack gave unauthorised access to customers' contact data. The authority found that the operator lacked technical and organisational measures appropriate to the risk, breaching Article 32(1)(b) and (2) GDPR. It fined the operator RON 25,376 (about EUR 5,000) and ordered it to revise and update its security incident response plan, including early threat detection and automated alerts through periodic system scanning. This is a press release, not the full decision.

The DPA fined a bank €500,000 for losing a customer’s documents when transporting them via a courier. The DPA held that the bank failed to ensure adequate security and proper supervision of its processor under Article 32 GDPR.

The DPA fined a genomics and biotechnology company €2.4 million for failing to adequately protect sensitive genetic and health data and for notifying the DPA about a personal data breach after the 72-hour deadline.

The Belgian DPA reprimanded a mayor for unlawfully further processing contact details from the municipality’s dataset for direct marketing purposes, and the municipality for failing to fulfil its obligations regarding the role of its DPO.

The DPA held that the daughter of a deceased patient could not request access under Article 15 GDPR from a hospital regarding her deceased father’s cause of death, as the information refers to her father and the right of access is a strictly personal and non-transferable right.

The DPA held that an event organiser violated a customer’s right to privacy when it submitted them marketing emails without their prior consent and by sending them those emails in CC, disclosing their address to a large group of third parties.

The Romanian authority concluded an investigation into an energy supplier that had notified a personal data breach under Article 33. Customer account data (email addresses and passwords) of a significant number of people had been accessed without authorisation and exfiltrated. The authority found the company lacked appropriate technical and organisational security measures, in breach of Article 32(1)(b) and (2) GDPR. It fined the company 126,797 lei (about EUR 25,000) and ordered it to make multi-factor authentication mandatory for all users and to adopt other suitable security measures.

A health professional complained that the professional Order kept her disciplinary suspension on its online register after she had appealed to the central appeals commission, although the appeal suspends the measure. The Garante found the online publication had no legal basis, breached lawfulness and accuracy principles, and that the Order had not validly designated a Data Protection Officer or notified the Authority of the DPO's contact details. The complaint about sharing data with the national Federation was dismissed. The Garante fined the Order EUR 3,000 for each of the two conducts (EUR 6,000 total), ordered it to designate and publish a DPO and report back within 30 days, and ordered publication of the decision.

A nurse complained that the professional register published on the website of the Pisa nursing order showed every member's home address. The order first claimed the publication was lawful under the sector rules, then said an employee had mistakenly uploaded the full internal register instead of the reduced one, which was also indexed by search engines. The Garante found the processing unlawful for lack of a legal basis and breach of the lawfulness principle, since publishing home addresses was not necessary. It fined the order EUR 16,000 and ordered publication of the decision, with no further corrective measures since the conduct had ceased.

Two municipal employee unions reported to the Authority that a CCTV system had been installed at the municipal vehicle depot in Moschato-Tavros and was allegedly used to monitor workers. After several exchanges and a hearing, the Authority found breaches of data minimisation, accountability, data protection by design, transparency and information duties, and of the records of processing requirement. It imposed two fines, EUR 7,000 and EUR 3,000 (EUR 10,000 in total), and a reprimand for Article 30.

FT Solutions, a company that runs the CercanumeriPro website selling lists of phone numbers to estate agents and debt collectors for marketing, was inspected by the Garante after complaints about unwanted calls. The company had labelled itself a processor, but the Garante found it was an independent controller. It had bought lists from an Irish provider without checking consent, processed inaccurate data, ignored data subject requests, gave poor transparency and used a wrong legal basis, and had weak access controls. The Garante banned further processing without valid consent, ordered several corrective measures, and fined the company EUR 5,000, also ordering publication of the decision.
The DPA issued a warning against a company. The company's website provided incorrect information on the use of cookies and stored cookie preferences unnecessarily.

The DPA held that a legal person does not have standing to bring a complaint under the GDPR, because the regulation’s scope only covers natural persons. Legal persons may, however, assert certain rights under national data protection law.

The DPA found Microsoft, the school, and the Ministry of Education in violation of information obligations under the GDPR. They also found unlawful processing of non-essential tracking cookies, ordering immediate deletion of data relating to cookies.
The DPA reprimanded a company for unlawfully retaining a former employee’s email account and phone number after the employment ended.
The DPA held that a business operator lawfully rejected an erasure request by one of its prior members since the remaining personal data was necessary to enforce a ban against them.
The DPA ordered a company to delete all personal data collected from the electronic land register or, in case of refusal, to provide the legal basis under which it continues to process the data.

A complaint about a courier who disclosed a recipient's name and surname to another company led the Spanish AEPD to open sanction proceedings against SEUR GEOPOST, S.L. The AEPD found that SEUR had no data processing contract with CITIBOX (Article 28 GDPR) and that its courier breached confidentiality (Article 5(1)(f) GDPR). SEUR paid voluntarily and got the 20% reduction, so the reduced fine is EUR 164,000, and it must show within 3 months that it has signed a processor contract with CITIBOX.

The DPA reprimanded a public authority for failing to ensure that international personal data transfers complied with the requirements in Chapter V of the GDPR, ordering proper assessment and safeguards.

The DPA ordered a temporal ban of the processing of personal data on ClothOff, a website that generates "deep nudes". It found that its operator failed to take effective protective measures for minors and to label the images as artificial effectively.

The Hamburg data protection authority fined a financial-sector company EUR 492,000 for infringing customers' rights in automated individual decisions. Credit card applications of several customers with good creditworthiness were rejected by algorithm without human involvement. When the customers asked for reasons, the company did not adequately meet its information and access duties, including meaningful information on the logic involved. The company's extensive efforts to improve its process and its full cooperation were weighed as substantially mitigating, and it accepted the fine notice. The release also gives a mid-year summary of fines in 2025, totalling about EUR 775,000, including a separate EUR 195,000 fine on a retail company.

This is a mid-year press release from the Hamburg DPA covering several fines issued in 2025, totalling about EUR 775,000. The part matching this Fino entry concerns a retail company that hired service providers to send postal advertising and, in several cases and over a longer period, failed to answer data subjects' rights requests on time. The authority fined it EUR 195,000. The release also describes a EUR 492,000 fine against a financial company over non-transparent automated decisions, plus smaller fines for email advertising without consent and for employees' unauthorised database look-ups.
The DPA issued a warning to a controller for sending an email to 450 individuals and companies using the CC instead of the BCC feature, which constituted a data breach.
The DPA dismissed a complaint, finding that the processing of personal data was necessary for creditworthiness assessment and that no right to erasure arose under Article 17 GDPR.

The DPA held that a credit information agency violated the prohibition of automated individual decision-making (ADM) by calculating a data subject’s creditworthiness leading to an energy provider’s decision not to conclude a contract with the data subject. The energy provider’s rejection also constituted ADM but was considered necessary for entering into a contract.

Following a personal data breach notification, the Romanian authority investigated an e-commerce operator whose platform was hit by a cyberattack exposing customers' payment card data. It found the site ran an outdated version of its platform without adequate security measures. The operator was fined RON 101,544 (about EUR 20,000) for breaching Article 32 GDPR. It was also ordered to implement a logging system for all access to its e-commerce platform, with backups of the logs. The operator has paid the fine.
A DPA imposed a €3,000 fine on a public authority for unlawfully publishing information about an employee’s ongoing criminal procedure and for failing to respond to their erasure request.

A real estate agency affiliated with Tecnocasa sent two unsolicited promotional emails to a property owner without consent. It ignored his erasure request and gave only vague answers to the Garante, claiming errors and oversights. The company had already been reprimanded and ordered in 2021 for similar conduct, and had not complied. The Garante found violations of Article 6(1)(a), Articles 12(3) and 17 and Article 58(2)(d) GDPR, and fined the company EUR 10,000, with publication of the decision.

The DPA fined the Province of Bolzano €32,000 for unlawfully operating a network of cameras monitoring traffic flows. The province had no valid legal basis for the involved processing of personal data, in particular license plates.

An employee complained that the company had created a work email account in his name without telling him, and that the account was used by many other people. The Garante found that the account, active from October 2019 to February 2023, was in practice a shared account used by employees and logistics contractors. It found breaches of the data protection principles and of the lawfulness and information duties, closed the allegations on Articles 25 and 32, ordered the company to prepare compliant information documents on corporate email accounts, and imposed a fine of EUR 15,000.

The Italian DPA investigated E-Power S.r.l., an energy/photovoltaic seller, after many complaints about unsolicited promotional calls made without a valid legal basis, including to numbers on the public opposition register, and an unanswered rights request. The company bought contact lists from a Moldovan list provider without checking their origin or consent, wrongly treated roles, and had a deficient website contact form. The Authority dropped the charge on late replies to its information requests, but found the other violations proven. It fined the company EUR 35,000, banned further processing of the complainants' data, ordered compliance measures and ordered publication of the decision.

A hospital employee complained that details of her miscarriage, treated at the hospital where she works, had circulated among colleagues. The complaint pointed to access to the hospital's health dossier through a generic radiology account. The Garante's investigation found that the hospital's health dossier was configured in breach of the basic processing principles, security and privacy by design rules and its 2015 dossier guidelines. It declared the processing unlawful, fined the hospital EUR 20,000 and ordered it to remove the 'pharmacovigilance' access mode and restrict a nursing profile's access. The hospital must also report on its measures within 90 days. The decision is to be published.

The DPA held that a news broadcaster lawfully produced and published a video depicting a political gathering engaging in anti-democratic behaviour since the processing was carried out for journalistic purposes.

The DPA held that a lawyer, acting as a data controller, lawfully requested user profile data from an online platform and disclosed it in civil proceedings. The processing was justified, as it served the lawyer’s legitimate interests in representing his client.

After a press article and an employee complaint, the CNIL inspected the Samaritaine department store, which had installed five cameras disguised as smoke detectors, with microphones, in two stockrooms in August 2023 to deal with thefts. The restricted committee found the covert filming and sound recording of employees unfair and undocumented (not in the records or the DPIA, DPO not informed), as well as excessive data collection, and also found breaches of Articles 33(1), 33(5) and 38(1). It described the company's conduct as clearly negligent. It imposed an administrative fine of EUR 100,000 and ordered publication, with the company no longer named after two years.

In December 2023 Servicios Financieros Carrefour notified the AEPD of a cyber incident in which an attacker used compromised credentials to extract customer personal data, including financial and payment-related data. The AEPD opened a sanction procedure alleging a breach of Article 5(1)(f) GDPR, because appropriate security measures were not in place, and proposed a fine of EUR 2,500,000. The company acknowledged responsibility and paid voluntarily on 27 August 2025, receiving two 20% reductions. The AEPD confirmed the infringement and set the final fine at EUR 1,500,000, ending the procedure.

The Italian DPA inspected a nursing home in Rome (Casa di Cura Città di Roma) on its electronic health record (dossier sanitario). It found that nurses, doctors and administrative staff could see data of patients well beyond what they needed, including after consent was withdrawn. Read-access logging was missing, with no alerts, no log checks, no penetration tests and no training on the dossier. The Authority declared the processing unlawful under Articles 5, 9, 25 and 32 GDPR and fined the clinic EUR 12,000, treating the seriousness as medium. It ordered no corrective measures because the clinic had already fixed the problems, and it ordered publication of the order.

An employee of the Florence Fire Brigade Command complained that a spreadsheet with colleagues' names, vaccination status and health-related notes was posted on the Command's Telegram channel, which had about 260 members. The Ministry said a staff member posted the file by mistake and removed it after about 5 minutes. The Garante found the processing unlawful, since there was no suitable legal basis and the data went to people not authorised to see it. It fined the Ministry EUR 12,000 and ordered publication of the order. It found no need for further corrective measures.

A candidate for the post of director of a regional park authority complained that the minutes of the selection committee, containing personal data of all 45 candidates, had been published on the authority's website and indexed by search engines. The minutes also included self-declarations about pending criminal proceedings or convictions for seven candidates. The authority said it was a clerical error and removed and de-indexed the documents quickly. The Garante found the disclosure had no legal basis and breached lawfulness principles and the rules on criminal-conviction data. It imposed a fine of EUR 8,000 and ordered publication of the decision.

The Garante received reports that the Municipality of Buccino had published on its Facebook page many photos of minors and of people with mental disabilities. It also found that the Municipality had not published the contact details of its data protection officer. The Municipality did not follow up the hearing invitation and filed no defence after the supplementary notice. The Garante found breaches of the lawfulness and minimisation principles, the special-category rules, and the DPO publication duties. It fined the Municipality EUR 4,000 for the Facebook publications and EUR 2,000 for the DPO omission, total EUR 6,000, ordered it to stop the dissemination and publish the DPO contact details, and ordered publication of the decision.

Following an inspection by the Guardia di finanza, the Garante found that a company operated video surveillance systems in two shops in Carmagnola (3 and 4 cameras) without adequate information signs and without the Labour Inspectorate authorisation required by Article 4 of Law 300/1970. The company filed no defence. The Garante declared the processing unlawful under Articles 5(1)(a) and 13 GDPR and Article 114 of the Code. It imposed a fine of EUR 6,000 and ordered publication of the decision.

A former employee of the municipality of Nichelino complained that her request to rectify two published decisions was not answered. The decisions, which stated she failed her probation, stayed online far too long. The Garante also found that the municipality kept intermediate and final rankings of a public competition online with excessive candidate data. It found breaches of lawfulness, minimisation, legal basis and the data subject's rectification right. It imposed two fines, EUR 10,000 and EUR 8,000, totalling EUR 18,000, and ordered publication of the decision.

The DPA imposed a temporary ban on "FaceBoarding", a facial recognition system used for passenger identification in airports. It found that the controller had not implemented adequate security measures.

The DPA found that a restaurant owner unlawfully recorded data subjects on a public street and monitored employees and guests without a valid legal basis. The DPA prohibited the continued use of the CCTV system and stressed that any future surveillance must comply with GDPR principles.

The Romanian DPA finished an investigation in August 2025 into Unita Turism Holding S.A., which had notified a personal data breach under Article 33 GDPR. A cyber attack led to unauthorised disclosure and extraction of data on current and former employees, including national ID numbers, medical and bank/financial documents. The investigation found the controller did not have appropriate technical and organisational security measures in place at the time of the attack. It was fined RON 25,368 (stated as equivalent to EUR 5,000), and the fine has been paid.

The DPA fined a bank €1,800,000 for failing to implement sufficient technical and organisational measures regarding a new login feature on their app, which led to unauthorised access to customers' accounts by third parties.
The DPA issued a warning to a company engaging in direct marketing for failing to respond to a data subject’s requests to access and erasure. The DPA announced a fine in case the violation continues.

This is a newsletter item summarising a penalty decision (Straferkenntnis) of the Austrian DPA of 5 September 2025 against a bakery company. For more than a year the company ran 30 insufficiently signposted video cameras across several bakery sites, covering customer areas, public areas and staff-only areas, and the settings were not the least intrusive means in time or place. Passers-by, customers and employees were filmed without a justifying basis. In at least one case footage was also passed on via a messenger service, contrary to the purpose-limitation rule. The authority imposed a fine of EUR 33,500; the decision is not yet final.

A tenant complained to the Belgian DPA about the unlawful use of four surveillance cameras in and around a student house. After an inspection, the Litigation Chamber found the landlord had no valid legal basis for the cameras, breached the accountability principle, filmed the public road and neighbours' property (data minimisation) and kept no processing register. It ordered the cameras switched off and the data deleted, issued a reprimand for the missing register, and imposed fines of EUR 8,000 and EUR 1,200 plus a EUR 500 increase for aggravating circumstances, totalling EUR 9,700. The transparency complaint was rejected.

Following data breach notifications from its processor Stratesys and controller SAREB after a cyberattack, the Spanish DPA investigated security failures and the lack of a compliant data processing agreement. The AEPD found that SAREB breached Article 5(1)(f) GDPR due to insufficient technical and organizational security measures and excessive data retention, as well as Article 28 GDPR for lacking a compliant data processing agreement with Stratesys. SAREB acknowledged its responsibility and made voluntary payment of the proposed fines, benefiting from two cumulative 20% statutory reductions that reduced the initial penalty of EUR 300,000 to EUR 180,000. In its final decision, the AEPD terminated the proceedings, confirmed the EUR 180,000 fine, and ordered SAREB to demonstrate compliance with security measures and Article 28 requirements within three months.
The DPA imposed an administrative fine of € 870 on an advertising agency for failing to notify a personal data breach within 72 hours in violation of Article 33 GDPR.

The DPA found that an association unlawfully continued to process a former member's email address by keeping it in the recipient list of emails sent by other members of the association after the termination of her membership.

Following two CNIL inspection missions (2022 and 2023) on Gmail and on advertising cookies placed when creating a Google account, the restricted committee found that Google LLC and Google Ireland Limited breached Article 82 of the French Data Protection Act (cookies placed without valid consent, with an account-creation path biased towards accepting targeted advertising) and Article L. 34-5 of the postal and electronic communications code (ads inserted between Gmail emails without prior consent). It fined Google LLC EUR 200,000,000 and Google Ireland Limited EUR 125,000,000, using the Alphabet group turnover as the economic-unit basis. It also ordered both companies to comply, with a EUR 100,000 per day penalty after six months, and ordered publication of the decision.

The DPA reprimanded Microsoft for mishandling an access request filed by a data subject whose account was suspended after an alleged breach of the service agreement. Microsoft deleted the requested information after refusing to provide access and failed to inform the data subject about their right to file a complaint.

After a cyber-attack, La Fântâna S.R.L. notified a personal data breach to the Romanian authority. The investigation, finished in July 2025, found that the company did not have appropriate technical and organisational security measures in place when the attack happened. Card data of a significant number of people was disclosed, creating a risk of bank fraud. The company was fined RON 50,693 (about EUR 10,000) and has already paid it.

Following an online inspection of the shein.com website on 10 August 2023, the CNIL restricted committee found that the company placed advertising and other cookies on users' terminals without prior consent. It also found that refusal and withdrawal of consent were not effective and that consent was not informed because the third parties placing advertising cookies were not identified. The committee used the turnover of the parent company, as the economic unit, to set the fine. It imposed an administrative fine of EUR 150 million and ordered publication of the decision, which will no longer name the company after two years. No injunction was issued because the company had come into compliance during the proceedings.
The DPA fined a company €5,000 for calling a data subject for direct marketing purposes without their consent, in violation of national telecommunication laws.

The Polish DPA published news that it fined ING Bank Śląski PLN 18,416,400 for scanning identity documents of customers and prospective customers between 1 April 2019 and 23 September 2020. The bank did not assess whether scanning was necessary under AML rules and scanned documents even for matters such as ATM complaints. The President of UODO found a lack of legal basis and breaches of the principles of lawfulness, purpose limitation and data minimisation. The fine was considered effective, proportionate and dissuasive.
The DPA held that processing an ID card for the verification of a bike rental company’s customers was not necessary for the performance of the contract or for the purpose of fraud prevention.

The DPA reprimanded a politician for collecting a data subject’s email address from a public source and sending them political marketing, in violation of the principles of lawfulness, purpose limitation and transparency.

A guest who booked a villa complained that the company running it demanded a full copy of every guest's identity document for the traveller register sent to the Guardia Civil. The guest had offered to give just the data needed. The AEPD opened proceedings for breach of the data minimisation principle (Art. 5(1)(c) GDPR) and proposed a fine of EUR 70,000. The company acknowledged responsibility and paid voluntarily, so the two 20% reductions applied and the fine became EUR 42,000. The AEPD confirmed the infringement, closed the procedure and ordered the company to change its registration system and delete the ID copies it had collected.
The DPA held that using the last four digits of a personal identification number as a password for a document submitted to the data subject does not constitute processing of personal data.

After a ransomware attack that the club notified to the AEPD in October 2023, affecting data of about 60,000 people, the AEPD opened sanctioning proceedings. It proposed fines for breaching the integrity and confidentiality principle (Article 5(1)(f)) and for inadequate security of processing (Article 32). The club admitted responsibility and paid voluntarily, which gave two cumulative 20% reductions. The procedure was terminated with a reduced fine of 66,000 euros, and the club must also prove it has implemented adequate security measures.

The DPA issued a warning to the provider of a dentist appointment website. The controller had processed personal data in violation of the principles of lawfulness, transparency, purpose limitation and data minimisation.

The DPA fined a payment service provider €80,000 for failing to ensure security of processing in relation to a data breach affecting over 20,000 data subjects. Data subjects’ contact data were sold online, and the company did not take measures until a year later.
The DPA upheld a complaint regarding an access request, and ordered Google LLC to provide the data subject with a full copy of their personal data on YouTube.
The DPA upheld a complaint regarding an access request, and ordered Google LLC to provide the data subject with a full copy of their personal data on YouTube.

The DPA fined a media company €6,820 for failing to bring its cookie banner into compliance by implementing a visually equivalent option to reject cookies. The DPA previously ordered the controller to do so in accordance with Article 58(2)(d) GDPR.

The DPA refused to comply with a request under the national freedom of information regime and did not provide access to its findings connected to a data breach since this would harm the controller and might undermine trust in the DPA.

This text is the EDPB Annual Report 2025, not the Cypriot decision itself. It has a short entry on a case against Bank of Cyprus Public Company Limited, which concerned a personal data breach notification and a breach of data availability and confidentiality. The Cypriot authority decided on 5 August 2025 that Articles 5(1)(f), 24 and 32 GDPR had been infringed, and imposed an administrative fine of EUR 25,000. The report gives no reasoning, calculation or orders.

The DPA reprimanded the Border Police over its failure to report a data breach to the DPA and the affected data subject. The DPA clarified that data breaches involving identification documents entail a high risk for data subjects.

A doctor's private car, carrying unsecured medical records of eight patients from home visits, was stolen. The health care institution reported the breach to the data protection authority, which found that its risk analysis was incomplete and no adequate safeguards existed for records taken on home visits. The President of UODO fined the institution PLN 32,832 for the inadequate risk analysis and security measures, not for the loss of data itself. After the theft the institution updated its policy, trained staff and gave doctors combination-lock folders.

After press reports and some reports, the Italian DPA opened an ex officio investigation into the City of Venice's online portal for the access contribution to the historic city, where visitors pre-register to claim exclusions or exemptions. It found the processing breached the principles of lawfulness, purpose limitation, minimisation, storage limitation, integrity and confidentiality, and privacy by design and by default, plus security. It fined the Municipality EUR 10,000 and ordered corrective measures, such as reducing pre-registration, widening the generic 'other exemptions' category, suspending collection of data on guests invited by residents, and regulating follow-up checks. The Venice Tribunal later rejected the opposition and fully confirmed the decision.

The Garante inspected Careggi University Hospital in Florence and found that its two applications for outpatient and inpatient records worked as a 'health dossier' without proper information to patients, consent, granular blackout options, access alerts or clear authorisation rules. The processing ran from 2011 to 2025 and affected a large number of patients. The hospital adopted corrective measures only after the inspection, so the Garante imposed no further corrective measures. It declared the processing unlawful under Articles 5(1)(a) and (f), 9, 25 and 32 GDPR and fined the hospital. The Florence Tribunal later reduced the fine to EUR 20,000 (judgment 1947/2026 of 9 April 2026); the Garante's published text shows only the reduced amount.
The DPA held that Vinted unlawfully collected a user's phone number for the purpose of account verification.
The DPA clarified that under the accountability principle, controllers must sometimes deviate from their general data retention policies in order to demonstrate compliance.
The DPA ordered the Estonian Public Broadcaster to remove a person's photos and their name from some articles since the depicted events no longer constitute public interest.
The DPA rejected a data subject’s complaint regarding his neighbor’s dummy CCTV system and held that the GDPR does not apply to dummy cameras since no processing takes place.

The UODO President fined a catering entrepreneur PLN 18,941 for failing to cooperate with the authority. The case began with a 2021 complaint by an employee about processing of her biometric data (probably fingerprints) by her employer. The entrepreneur never answered the authority's repeated requests for explanations, the last in May 2024, nor the notice of fine proceedings opened in January 2025. The President found this a conscious and deliberate refusal to cooperate, which counted as aggravating.
The DPA imposed a €4,000,000 fine on a communication network provider after inadequate security measures enabled a cyberattack and the unlawfully access of personal data.

After a cyber attack, Agricola International SA notified a personal data breach affecting many employees, their family members and customers. The Romanian authority's investigation, finished in June 2025, found that the company had no security measures requiring secure access to its network storage device. It found a breach of Article 32(1)(b) and (d) and (2) GDPR and imposed a contravention fine of 25,226.50 lei (about EUR 5,000). It also ordered technical and organisational measures under Article 58(2)(d). The company has already paid the fine.

The DPA fined a bank PLN 18,416,400 (approximately €4,300,000) over the excessive and unlawful processing of customers’ identity documents. The DPA clarified that AML legislation does not allow for the indiscriminate scanning of customers’ IDs.

The DPA held that an alleged offense by a child’s legal guardian or an order for limited contact does not automatically exclude the legal guardian from accessing any part of their child’s medical file on their behalf.

McDonald's Polska entrusted the processing of restaurant employees' scheduling data to an external PR firm, 24/7 Communication. Because of a misconfigured server, a file with employee data (including PESEL and passport numbers) was exposed in a publicly accessible directory. The UODO President found that neither the controller nor the processor carried out a risk analysis or implemented adequate safeguards, that the processor was not properly vetted or supervised, that no sub-processing contract existed, that the DPO was not involved, and that data minimisation was breached. McDonald's was fined a total of PLN 16,932,657 and reprimanded for not notifying former employees directly; the processor was fined PLN 183,858 in total.

This is a UODO news item about one case with two addressees. McDonald's Polska outsourced the handling of staff work schedules to the processor 24/7 Communication. A misconfigured server exposed a file containing employee data, including national ID (PESEL) and passport numbers, in a publicly accessible directory. Neither the controller nor the processor had carried out a risk analysis or put suitable measures in place, and the processor had no sub-processing contract with another company it used. The President of UODO fined McDonald's PLN 16,932,657 in total and reprimanded it, and fined the processor 24/7 Communication PLN 183,858 in total, made up of three fines (PLN 94,286, 42,429 and 47,143).

A publisher emailed about 55 recipients with all addresses visible in the 'To' field. The complainant, an author writing under a pseudonym, had his email address, full name, pseudonym, home address and tax number exposed, revealing his gender identity and belonging to a gender minority. The Authority found the publisher had no technical or organisational measures, and did not notify the Authority or the complainant of the breach. It imposed separate fines of EUR 3,000, 2,000 and 4,000 (EUR 9,000 in total) and ordered the publisher to draw up a personal data breach management policy.

The DPA dismissed a complaint against a dating app regarding an access request on the grounds that the violation had been remedied during the proceedings. However, the DPA ordered the company to extend the period of validity for the verification links used when handling access requests.
The DPA fined a utilities company €200,000 for mistakenly including personal data of a data subject in a third person’s contract, in violation of the principle of data accuracy.

The AEPD sanctioned TRIVE Credit Spain for failing to comply with its earlier final resolution ordering it to answer a data subject's access request. The company did not act after the AEPD sent two notices. The breach was of Art. 58(2)(c) GDPR, typified under Art. 83(6). The AEPD first proposed EUR 450,000, then EUR 225,000 after using the company's 2023 accounts, and refused to archive the case or give only a reprimand. TRIVE paid voluntarily on 12 June 2025 without admitting liability; the 20% reduction brought it to EUR 180,000.

A policyholder complained that NN Hellas and the dental services provider MEDIADENT never answered his repeated requests for access to recordings of his calls to the dental-care call centre. The Authority found that NN Hellas, as controller, infringed the right of access under Article 15(1) and (3) GDPR. It ordered NN Hellas to hand over the recordings or transcripts within 10 days and fined it EUR 20,000. MEDIADENT was separately fined EUR 2,000 for failing to cooperate with the Authority (Article 31), as it never replied or appeared.

An insurance company sent detailed information and documents on a customer's three life policies to an email address that was not hers. The requests came from a third party who impersonated her, using a forged handwritten signature and precise details. The company only realised after she disowned the address in September 2024, and it notified the breach to the Garante about four months later. The Garante found breaches of the lawfulness and confidentiality principles and of the breach-notification duty, and fined the company EUR 80,000.

A trade union reported that Magna PT S.p.A. made workers fill in a 'return to work interview' form with their manager after absences for illness, injury or hospitalisation. The Garante found that the form collected health data and that the processing breached the data protection principles, the legal basis rules, the special-category rules, the information duty and the employment-data rules. It banned further processing of the data collected through the forms, ordered their deletion within 60 days, and imposed a fine of EUR 50,000. The fine reflected the seriousness, health data, duration since at least 2020 and ongoing, and the large number of workers affected, with cooperation noted.

A contract lecturer filed three joined complaints against his university. The Garante found that the university kept the lecturer's mailbox and its messages for about two years after the work relationship ended, and for a period did not tell senders that he no longer had access. It also found failures in handling the lecturer's rights requests and in the online publication of his data. The Garante treated these as two separate conducts and fined EUR 4,000 for each, EUR 8,000 in total, and ordered publication of the decision. No further corrective measures were imposed because the effects had ceased.

Parents complained that a school published on its website a circular convening the inclusion working groups (GLO), listing pupils with disabilities by surname, first initial and class, including their child. The school said an administrative assistant posted it in the wrong website section by mistake, against the head teacher's instructions, and removed it after about 28 days. The Garante held that the school, as controller, is responsible for its staff's errors and unlawfully disseminated health data without a legal basis. It fined the school EUR 4,000 and ordered publication of the decision, with no further corrective measures since the conduct had ended.

A parent complained that a nursery school made enrolment depend on accepting a privacy notice that included consent to use the child's images, and that it ran CCTV filming children and staff. The Garante's checks also found many photos of identifiable infants, including in sensitive moments, published on the nursery's website. It found unlawful processing: no valid legal basis or consent, deficient information notices, no data protection impact assessment for the CCTV, and an improperly designated DPO (the school head, in a conflict of interest). It fined the nursery EUR 10,000, ordered a ban on further processing of the children's photos (including online) and their deletion from its archives, and ordered publication of the decision.

A bank customer who had been the victim of a fraud asked the bank for access to recordings of his calls to its customer service on one evening. The bank first said only one silent call existed and sent the other recordings only after the complaint to the Garante and the opening of proceedings, which it blamed on human error and outsourcer process changes. The Garante found breaches of Articles 12(3), 12(4) and 15 GDPR, taking account of the single data subject, cooperation, and the corrective measures taken. It fined the bank EUR 100,000 and ordered publication of the decision.

The DPA held that the customer of a company had a right to revoke her consent to the use of her image for the company's advertising. The DPA also clarified that consent can be revoked regardless of negative economic consequences for the controller.

The press release announces eight new administrative fines totalling EUR 350,500 and highlights the two largest. After an anonymous report of a leak of personal data of over a million vehicle owners, the Agency investigated the Croatian Insurance Bureau (HUO) and found its database matched the leaked data. HUO had not taken appropriate organisational and technical security measures and had not set maximum retention periods for data in its Information Centre register. Because HUO is a legal person with public powers, the fine was limited under the national implementation law and set at EUR 101,000. The release also covers a EUR 175,000 fine on a sports betting operator, which is a separate case.

The DPA issued a warning to a controller for failing to inform a data subject on the actions taken following their objection to the processing of their personal data for direct marketing within one month.

The UODO President fined a children's university hospital in Białystok PLN 66,500 after a ransomware attack that blocked access to its IT systems and affected the confidentiality and availability of data of about 2,000 employees. The authority found the hospital's risk analysis was flawed: it assessed risk from the hospital's perspective rather than that of data subjects, did not link processing to threats, and its proposed measures were vague. The hospital also relied on a cybersecurity-law audit, lacked backup restore testing procedures and could not document regular testing of security measures, contrary to accountability. This text is a news item summarising the decision.
The DPA fined a company operating sports centres €96,000 for implementing mandatory facial recognition systems to enter and exit the premises, without the prior knowledge or consent of its members.

Decision 27/2025 of the Greek data protection authority. A woman complained that at least 15 prepaid mobile numbers had been registered in her name, using her ID data, without her knowledge. The activations were made by DS Phone, a Vodafone franchisee acting as its processor, and she was later summoned by prosecutors as a suspect in fraud investigations. Under the GDPR the authority fined Vodafone-Panafon EUR 350,000 for failing in its duties towards its processor (Art. 28) and EUR 200,000 for keeping inaccurate data (Art. 5(1)(d)): EUR 550,000 in all, the figure shown. It added a EUR 150,000 fine under the national e-privacy law (Law 3471/2006) for inadequate security measures, fined the processor DS Phone EUR 40,000, and warned Vodafone to introduce stronger technical measures such as an SMS alert to the subscriber.

A Vodafone subscriber complained that unknown persons had registered at least 15 prepaid mobile numbers in her name using her ID data. It emerged that the franchise shop DS Phone, acting as Vodafone's processor, had activated 14 prepaid lines for a tourist group by attaching the complainant's ID file from an earlier visit to another shop, by mistake. The Authority found DS Phone infringed Articles 32 and 29 GDPR and fined it EUR 40,000. It also fined Vodafone separately (EUR 350,000, EUR 200,000 and EUR 150,000) and issued a warning to it; those parts concern Vodafone, not DS Phone.

The DPA reprimanded the Danish Agency for Digitalization for the insecure processing of personal data via its digital post system, in violation of Article 32 GDPR. The system suffered five data breaches that affected hundreds of thousands of data subjects.

A hospital doctor complained that the head of his clinic collected and used statistics on his operating times, overtime and material use, named per doctor, to exclude him from a hospital laboratory, without informing him, and that his access request went unanswered. The Authority rejected the complaint as inadmissible against the clinic head personally, and held the hospital liable as controller. It fined the hospital EUR 7,000 in total: EUR 4,000 for breaching Article 5, EUR 1,500 for Article 14 and EUR 1,500 for Article 15. It also reprimanded the hospital for breaching Article 31 (late cooperation with the Authority).

The DPA fined an association for people with autism €10,000 for failing to comply with an access request by the legal guardians of a child and for unlawfully transmitting the child’s personal data to third parties.

The DPA fined a company that provides 'after adoption' services GBP 18,000 (€20,707) for the unlawfully destruction of irreplaceable records related to adoptions. It found that the company failed to ensure appropriate security and organisational measures and violated the principle of accountability.

The Irish DPC announced its final decision on an inquiry into a personal data breach at CDETB, where a webserver retained grant applicants' personal data and malware was found on it. The DPC found infringements of the security principle and security measures (Arts 5(1)(f), 32(1), 32(2)), late notification to the DPC (Art 33(1)), and failures to notify data subjects (Art 34(1) and 34(4)). It reprimanded CDETB, imposed fines totalling EUR 125,000 and ordered it to bring its processing into compliance. The fine was well below the draft range of up to EUR 210,000 because CDETB accepted the findings, took responsibility, apologised and took steps to prevent recurrence.

ANSPDCP finished an investigation into Vodafone Romania in May 2025, started after the company notified a personal data breach under Article 33 GDPR. It found that Vodafone had not put in place appropriate technical and organisational measures for data protection by design and by default, which led to unauthorised disclosure of and access to customers' data. Vodafone was fined RON 20,226 (about EUR 4,000) and ordered to implement a mechanism for regularly testing and assessing the effectiveness of its security measures.

A complainant received information letters from Piraeus Bank treating him as a guarantor of a relative's business loan, although he had no such role; a bank employee had entered him wrongly in the system. The bank sent a third letter even after he objected. The authority found no proof that his data were passed to the special purpose entity or to the servicer Intrum, and found no breach of the right to object (Art. 21) and no breach by Intrum. It found the bank processed inaccurate data without a legal basis, breaching Articles 5(1)(a), 5(1)(d) and 6(1), and fined it EUR 50,000.

The DPA warned a municipality for unlawfully publishing personal data of a former town councilor and clarified that the publication was not covered by transparency obligations under national administrative law.

In a case involving two neighbours, the DPA held that the one-time collection of personal data via an aerial drone, in order to collect proof for court proceedings, fell under the household exemption of the GDPR.

A parent complained that footage of their minor daughter, recorded at a school, had left the school's custody and ended up with the Guardia Civil, and that the recordings were made without consent or information. The Spanish AEPD opened a sanctioning procedure against the school for breaches of Article 5(1)(f), Article 6(1) and Article 13 GDPR, with a proposed fine of EUR 40,000. The school acknowledged responsibility and paid, taking two 20% reductions, so the reduced fine is EUR 24,000. The decision terminates the procedure and orders the school to show security measures, stop the unlawful recording and provide the required information within three months.

A ferry captain employed by a contractor of Stockholm public transport company SL complained about mandatory breathalyser tests before each departure, whose results were logged. IMY found that SL processed the complainant's data between October 2021 and August 2022 without a legal basis under Article 6 and, as health data, without any Article 9(2) exemption. It treated the violations as low severity but not minor enough for a reprimand, found SL negligent, and imposed an administrative fine of SEK 75,000.

IMY investigated a complaint from a ship's master employed by a contractor of the Stockholm public transport authority, about daily breathalyser tests with logged results. IMY found that the company Waxholms Ångfartygs AB processed the complainant's data without a legal basis under Article 6 and processed sensitive health data without any Article 9(2) exception applying, in 2020 and 2021-2022. The violations were assessed as low severity, since the aim was transport safety and the complainant was not directly identifiable. IMY rejected a reprimand and imposed an administrative fine of SEK 75,000. The maximum was calculated on the turnover of the whole SL group, treated as one undertaking.

The DPA issued a warning against the deployment of a “Smart Policing” system by the Hellenic Police, involving smart portable devices used by patrols to determent and verify the identity of citizens subject to on-the-spot checks via the use of biometric data. The DPA considers this processing of personal data unlawful.
Following an ex officio investigation, the DPA ordered a medical services provider to set storage periods for documents related to the processing of access requests.
The DPA fined a utilities company €3,000 for processing data without a legal basis, violating Article 6(1) GDPR.
The DPA fined a processor €12,000 for subcontracting another processor without the authorisation of the controller in violation of Article 28(2) GDPR.

The DPA fined a cinema chain €18,000 for automatically including another person's personal data during a customer’s purchase of movie tickets using the controller’s app, in violation of the principles of data accuracy and security of processing.

The DPA held that information about visits to a website’s subpages, containing content on particular medical issues, constitute sensitive data. Therefore, the DPA reprimanded a company for unlawfully processing this sensitive information via the Meta pixel.

The Norwegian DPA carried out a digital inspection of six websites' use of tracking tools. On the children's helpline website 116111.no, run by Kristiansand municipality, it found Meta Pixel and Snap Pixel sending visitors' data to Meta and Snap without a valid legal basis, and the privacy notice did not mention the pixels or the sharing. The DPA fined the municipality NOK 250,000 for breaching Article 6(1) and the information duties in Articles 12(1) and 13. In setting the amount it weighed the importance of the service for vulnerable children, the municipality's strained finances and its clean-up measures. The municipality had removed the pixels after the notice of decision.

A former customer received a postal letter from CaixaBank concerning privacy policy updates and commercial profiling, despite having terminated their contractual relationship in 2008. The customer made an access request and then submitted a complaint to the AEPD. CaixaBank argued that retention was justified under Article 6(1)(b) GDPR based on an open credit line with a maturity date in 2030, but the AEPD found that the mortgage credit agreement had been formally cancelled in February 2008. Holding the complainant's data for almost 16 years without a valid purpose violated the storage limitation principle, and the AEPD imposed a fine of EUR 200,000 for infringing Article 5(1)(e) GDPR.
The DPA reprimanded a daycare center and its debt collection agency for unlawfully processing incorrect information about outstanding debt and failure to delete incorrect information.

The ICO investigated, jointly with the Canadian privacy regulator, a 2023 credential stuffing attack on the US genetic testing company 23andMe in which a threat actor accessed customer accounts and genetic and health data. It found that 23andMe failed to implement adequate authentication (such as mandatory MFA), extra protection for raw genetic data, preparation for credential stuffing, and effective monitoring and detection. These failures breached the UK GDPR security principle and Article 32. The ICO imposed a penalty of £2,310,000, set with regard to the company's significantly deteriorated financial position. By 31 December 2024 the infringements had been remedied, so no enforcement notice was given.

A complainant received numerous unsolicited promotional emails for the website noicompriamoauto.it, sent by third-party partners acting for the company, and had also not received a timely answer to his rights request. The Garante found the company to be the controller, that it had not properly regulated its relationships with the partners, had not supervised them, could not prove valid consent, and had made it hard to exercise rights. It imposed a fine of EUR 45,000 and ordered publication of the decision. No corrective measures were added because the company had ended the partner contracts and the email campaigns.

The DPA fined a consulting firm €21,000 for unintentionally disclosing personal data of numerous job applicants to the other applicants due to linking to an internal Google spreadsheet in the communication with the applicants. Thus, violating Article 5(1)(f) GDPR.

Following an ex officio investigation, the DPA warned a car retailer for violations relating to its website's cookies. In particular, the controller failed to inform data subjects that they could reject cookies by closing the cookie banner.
The DPA issued a warning against a car dealership for implementing a non-compliant cookie banner on its website. The banner did not include an option for rejecting unnecessary cookies.

The DPA found that a controller failed to respond to a data subject’s access request in time and failed to provide them with a full copy of their personal data, in violation of Article 12 and Article 15 GDPR.

The DPA fined a car rental company €100,000 for processing information about customers’ previous incidents in blacklists without a legal basis. Being blacklisted led to the denial of services by the rental company.
The DPA reprimanded a company for failing to respond to an access request. Specifically, the controller did not confirm that it did not process personal data referring to the data subject.
The DPA fined a company €3,000 for the use of non-essential cookies on their website without the user's prior consent and for two other cookie-related infractions.
The DPA fined a telecommunications company €200,000 for issuing a duplicate of a data subject’s SIM card to a third person without the knowledge or consent of the data subject.

This is the AEPD's ruling on the telecom operator DIGI's appeal for reconsideration (recurso de reposición) against the AEPD's resolution of 8 November 2024. That resolution fined DIGI EUR 200,000 for infringing Article 6(1) GDPR. A third party obtained a duplicate SIM card for the complainant at a DIGI point of sale on 6 April 2021, leaving the complainant without service. DIGI argued that it had followed its procedure, that it was being held strictly liable, that the fine was disproportionate, and that mitigating factors applied. The AEPD rejected every argument, found that no new facts or legal arguments had been raised, dismissed the appeal and left the EUR 200,000 fine in place.

ANSPDCP finished an investigation in April 2025 into an insurance broker that had notified a personal data breach after a cyber attack. Personal data of a significant number of clients, including national ID numbers, ID card photos, driving licences and contact details, was affected. The authority found that the broker had no security measures requiring secure access to its network storage equipment, so it had not ensured a level of security appropriate to the risk. It found a breach of Article 32(1)(b) and (2) GDPR and fined the broker RON 24,887 (about EUR 5,000).

The DPA fined an employer €42,000 for unlawfully adding a former employee’s personal mobile number to a WhatsApp group for employees after the employee explicitly opposed to use her private phone number for work-related communication.
The DPA imposed a €1,100,000 fine to an online pharmacy that made its customers identifiable by sharing their data with third-party tracking services.

The DPA fined an energy provider €1,380,000 for mistakenly attributing a data subject with another client’s gas supply contract and billing them based on the wrong contract, in violation of data accuracy and security of processing.

The DPA fined an electrical services company €10,000 for transferring the data subject's personal data to a grants management company without a valid legal basis. The former made a list of its customers available to a third party as part of an outsourcing arrangement.

The DPA fined Autostrade per l'Italia €420,000 for unlawfully processing an employee's personal data for disciplinary proceedings. The data included screenshots from the employee's social media account and private communications.
